paragraphs: This paper studies how to move probability mass from a continuous distribution to a collection of discrete destinations at minimum cost. In the setting considered first, moving mass costs the squared distance it travels. The authors extend a combinatorial approach previously used for transport between two discrete distributions to this mixed continuous-and-discrete problem.

For two-dimensional distributions, their algorithm computes a transport plan whose cost is within an additive epsilon of optimal. Its worst-case running time is O(n⁴ log n log(1/epsilon)), where n counts the discrete destinations. This guarantee assumes that the continuous distribution’s mass inside any triangle can be computed in constant time. It requires no smoothness assumption on that distribution.

The authors also develop a linear-space data structure for answering transport queries against a large discrete distribution. In two dimensions, queries take O(k³√N log(1/epsilon)) time, with N stored points and k query points. They report faster algorithms than previously known and describe extensions to higher dimensions and other Wasserstein transport costs.
neurips-2024-a-combinatorial-algorithm-f.tldr: A combinatorial framework gives approximate transport algorithms with explicit runtime guarantees and no smoothness requirement on the continuous distribution.

paragraphs: AdaNCA addresses a gap between image classification performance and robustness in Vision Transformers. Adding local information through convolutions or regional attention can improve feature aggregation without reliably improving resilience to challenging inputs. The paper instead introduces neural cellular automata as adapters placed between Transformer layers.

These automata build broader visual representations through local interactions among visual tokens. The approach uses this interaction mechanism to improve performance under adversarial perturbations and inputs outside the training distribution. Because standard neural cellular automata can be computationally expensive, the authors introduce Dynamic Interaction to make their interaction learning more efficient. They also analyze how adapter placement relates to robustness and develop an algorithm for selecting effective insertion locations.

On ImageNet1K, the paper reports more than a 10-percentage-point improvement in accuracy under adversarial attacks while adding less than 3% to the parameter count. Evaluations across eight robustness benchmarks and four Vision Transformer architectures show consistent robustness improvements. These findings support the usefulness of the adapters across the tested architectures and robustness settings.
neurips-2024-adanca-neural-cellular-auto.tldr: AdaNCA inserts neural cellular automata between Vision Transformer layers to improve measured robustness with a small parameter increase.

paragraphs: Airborne laser scanning helps archaeologists reveal landscapes concealed beneath vegetation, but applying deep learning to these scans requires suitable labeled examples. Archaeoscape addresses the shortage of openly available resources annotated by experts. Its contribution centers on a dataset that connects archaeological interpretation with modern computer vision.

The dataset covers 888 square kilometers in Cambodia and includes 31,141 annotated archaeological features from the Angkorian period. The authors describe it as more than four times larger than comparable datasets and the first archaeological airborne-laser-scanning resource to make data, annotations, and models openly accessible together. This combination provides both material for learning and shared resources for evaluating analysis methods.

The paper benchmarks several recent segmentation models, demonstrating benefits from modern vision techniques while identifying the difficulty of recognizing subtle human-made structures beneath dense jungle canopy. The contribution therefore includes both a larger research resource and an evaluation of methods on its particular challenges. The authors intend this access to help connect traditional archaeological work with deep learning research.
neurips-2024-archaeoscape-bringing-aeria.tldr: Archaeoscape provides open laser-scanning data, expert annotations, and models for detecting archaeological features beneath Cambodian jungle.

paragraphs: AvaTaR tackles the manual effort involved in prompting language-model agents to use external tools effectively. Access to tools and knowledge can improve an agent’s answers, but deciding how to instruct the agent remains a separate challenge. The paper proposes an automated framework that improves tool use for a specified task.

Its central component is a comparator that reasons about positive and negative examples sampled from training data. By contrasting these examples, the comparator develops prompts intended to guide the agent toward more effective behavior. This process repeats during optimization, making the comparison of successful and unsuccessful examples a source of increasingly informative instructions.

The authors evaluate AvaTaR on four multimodal retrieval datasets involving text, images, and relational information, plus three question-answering datasets. They report improvements over state-of-the-art approaches on all seven tasks and strong generalization to new cases. Average relative gains are 14% in retrieval Hit@1 and 13% on the question-answering datasets. These results support contrastive prompt optimization as a practical method for improving tool-using agents.
neurips-2024-avatar-optimizing-llm-agent.tldr: AvaTaR automatically improves tool-using agents by iteratively generating prompts from contrasts between positive and negative training examples.

paragraphs: AWT helps pretrained vision-language models recognize new concepts when information about the new classes is limited. Its approach expands the available evidence and organizes how the model uses it. The framework follows three stages: create varied inputs, assign them dynamic weights, and find semantic relationships between visual and language representations.

The augmentation stage uses image transformations to provide different visual perspectives and language models to enrich class descriptions. Weighting depends on prediction entropy, a measure of how spread out the model’s predictions are. Optimal transport then identifies semantic correlations in the shared vision-language space. Together, these stages aim to extract more useful information from the inputs available for adaptation.

AWT improves zero-shot use without additional training and supports few-shot learning through a multimodal adapter. The authors test image classification, video action recognition, and generalization outside the training distribution. They report consistent improvements over state-of-the-art methods in each evaluated setting, with further studies supporting adaptability across different vision-language models, architectures, and scales.
neurips-2024-awt-transferring-vision-lan.tldr: AWT combines input augmentation, uncertainty-based weighting, and optimal transport to improve vision-language model adaptation.

paragraphs: Principal component analysis is widely used to reduce dimensionality and suppress noise, but its effect on relationships between noisy observations is harder to quantify. This paper introduces a compression-ratio metric to describe how PCA changes distances. The goal is to make its denoising behavior more explicit for high-dimensional data.

For data with underlying communities, the authors show that PCA shrinks distances within a community substantially while shrinking distances between communities more mildly. They support this pattern with theoretical results and experiments on real data. The distinction matters because denoising can improve the separation of groups even when distances generally become smaller.

The authors then use variation in compression ratios to identify possible outliers. Their argument is that points with lower compression-ratio variance may lack a signal shared with other observations. They provide theoretical justification and simulations showing competitive outlier detection. On single-cell RNA sequencing datasets, removing points selected by this method improves clustering accuracy, connecting the proposed metric to a practical analysis task.
neurips-2024-capturing-the-denoising-eff.tldr: A compression-ratio metric explains PCA’s effect on community-structured noisy data and supports a competitive outlier-detection method.

paragraphs: This paper studies learning systems whose decisions change the environments that generate their future data. It considers multiple players acting independently to minimize private costs while satisfying coupled inequality constraints. Because their choices influence data distributions, the players must contend with feedback between deployed decisions and subsequent observations.

The authors analyze two equilibrium notions: performative stable equilibrium and Nash equilibrium. They establish sufficient conditions for existence and uniqueness and derive an upper bound on the distance between the two equilibria. This comparison is technically challenging because the joint cost function lacks strong convexity. The bound helps characterize how far these two notions of a settled outcome can differ in the studied setting.

The paper also develops a decentralized stochastic primal-dual algorithm to compute a performative stable equilibrium. Its analysis bounds the feedback effect and establishes sublinear convergence rates for performative regret and constraint violation. Under the analyzed conditions, the convergence order matches the case without performativity. Numerical experiments support the algorithm’s effectiveness and the theoretical results.
neurips-2024-decentralized-noncooperativ.tldr: The paper gives equilibrium guarantees and a decentralized learning algorithm for games where players’ decisions alter their data distributions.

paragraphs: Generative Fractional Diffusion Models change the noise dynamics underlying continuous-time score-based generation. The paper links some limitations of conventional diffusion models partly to Brownian motion’s independent increments. It replaces that process with an approximation to fractional Brownian motion, allowing noise increments to be correlated.

A parameter called the Hurst index controls these dynamics. At 0.5 it recovers ordinary Brownian motion; values above 0.5 introduce long-term memory and more regular paths. To make learning and inference tractable, the authors use a Markov approximation and derive its reverse-time model. They also introduce a continuous reparameterization and augmented score matching, taking advantage of a score function that is partly available in closed form.

The model offers another control through the number of Markov processes combined in the approximation. Evaluations on real image datasets show increased pixel-wise diversity and improved image quality according to lower FID. These findings support the proposed dynamics as a promising alternative, while the reported results specifically concern the evaluated image-generation settings.
neurips-2024-generative-fractional-diffu.tldr: Fractional diffusion models introduce controllable correlated noise and report improved image quality and pixel-wise diversity.

paragraphs: GeoTDM generates evolving three-dimensional geometric systems, extending the focus from individual structures to trajectories over time. Such trajectories must capture both spatial interactions and correspondence across successive moments. The paper also emphasizes physical symmetries, so that the representation of a system’s motion respects the relevant geometric transformations.

The authors theoretically show that diffusion models using equivariant temporal kernels can produce densities with the desired symmetry. They build a transition kernel combining SE(3)-equivariant spatial convolution with temporal attention. These components address geometric relationships and temporal dependencies together. For conditional generation, they introduce a learnable geometric prior into the forward diffusion process to make temporal conditioning more expressive.

Experiments cover both conditional and unconditional trajectory generation in physical simulation, molecular dynamics, and pedestrian motion. Across a broad set of evaluation metrics, the authors report realistic trajectories with significantly improved quality. The contribution is therefore both a symmetry-based theoretical justification and a concrete generative architecture evaluated on several types of dynamic geometric data.
neurips-2024-geometric-trajectory-diffus.tldr: GeoTDM combines symmetry-respecting spatial modeling and temporal attention to generate higher-quality three-dimensional trajectories in the evaluated settings.

paragraphs: Video text spotting requires a system to locate text, read it, and track it across frames. The authors identify limited recognition ability as a major bottleneck in a state-of-the-art video text spotter. GoMatching builds on an existing query-based image text spotter and concentrates training on tracking while preserving strong recognition.

The method adds a rescoring head that adjusts confidence scores for detected text instances through efficient tuning. This provides a better set of candidates for tracking. A second component, LST-Matcher, combines matches over short and long time spans using a Transformer. These two additions adapt the image model to video through candidate selection and temporal matching.

GoMatching achieves new records on ICDAR15-video, DSText, BOVText, and the paper’s new ArTVideo test set for arbitrarily shaped text. The evaluations cover dense, small, curved or otherwise irregular text, including Chinese and English. The authors also report substantial training-budget savings, supporting the practicality of focusing adaptation on tracking while retaining an effective image recognition component.
neurips-2024-gomatching-a-simple-baselin.tldr: GoMatching adapts an image text spotter to video with confidence rescoring and long- and short-term tracking matches.

paragraphs: This paper studies reinforcement learning with an infinite time horizon and an average-reward objective. In this undiscounted setting, the focus is sustained reward over time. The authors use kernel ridge regression to predict the expected value function, combining flexible function approximation with a framework suitable for mathematical analysis.

They propose an optimistic algorithm, similar in spirit to acquisition-function methods for bandit problems. Optimism uses uncertainty about predicted value to guide decisions toward potentially rewarding possibilities. The paper establishes no-regret performance guarantees under its kernel-based modeling assumptions. These guarantees concern how learning performance accumulates over time and depend on the stated modeling framework.

A second contribution is a new confidence interval for kernel-based predictions of the expected value function. This gives a way to express uncertainty around those predictions, which is directly relevant to an optimistic decision rule. The authors describe the interval as applicable across multiple reinforcement-learning problems, making it a broader analytical contribution alongside the particular average-reward algorithm.
neurips-2024-kernel-based-function-appro.tldr: An optimistic kernel-based reinforcement-learning algorithm receives no-regret guarantees for average reward under kernel modeling assumptions.

paragraphs: This paper asks whether images can be modeled effectively as one-dimensional causal sequences, an approach associated with language modeling. Vision systems usually use two-dimensional, non-causal processing, and this architectural difference complicates unified multimodal models. The authors investigate a specific obstacle to bringing visual representations into the causal sequence setting.

They identify an over-focus problem: attention concentrates too heavily on a small subset of visual tokens. This restricts feature diversity and weakens useful training gradients. De-focus Attention Networks use learnable bandpass filters to produce varied attention patterns. Training also includes large, scheduled drop-path rates and, for global understanding tasks, an auxiliary loss on globally pooled features.

These mechanisms encourage attention to cover more tokens and improve optimization. Experiments show that the resulting one-dimensional causal representations can perform comparably to two-dimensional non-causal representations on global perception, dense prediction, and multimodal understanding tasks. The findings support the feasibility of this modeling approach across the tested tasks and identify attention concentration as an actionable problem in making it work.
neurips-2024-learning-1d-causal-visual-r.tldr: De-focus Attention Networks spread attention across visual tokens, enabling competitive one-dimensional causal image representations in the tested tasks.

paragraphs: This paper investigates whether learned predictions can improve algorithms for difficult offline optimization problems. Earlier work largely studied online problems, where predictions offer information about a future that has not yet been observed. Here, the obstacle is computational: even with the problem instance available, finding sufficiently good solutions can face approximation-hardness barriers.

The authors consider supplying an algorithm with noisy predictions about an optimal solution. Their results show that this extra information can enable approximation performance beyond classical hardness thresholds for maximum cut and, more generally, maximization versions of constraint satisfaction problems. The predictions need not be perfectly correct for the paper’s approach to provide an advantage.

The significance lies in changing what information the optimization algorithm receives. Classical hardness results concern their original computational setting; learned guidance supplies additional information about the solution. The paper therefore establishes a role for predictions in addressing offline computational barriers, extending the learning-augmented perspective beyond its more common use in handling uncertainty about future inputs.
neurips-2024-learning-augmented-approxim.tldr: Noisy predictions about optimal solutions can help approximation algorithms surpass classical hardness thresholds for maximum cut and related problems.

paragraphs: Double descent describes a generalization pattern with an error peak between two improving regions. Prior work discussed in this paper associates the phenomenon with over-parameterized models, while treating the under-parameterized regime through the usual bias-variance trade-off. The authors examine whether that distinction captures all possible behavior in least-squares regression.

They present two simple examples and prove that both exhibit double descent while remaining under-parameterized. These constructions establish that the phenomenon can occur in this regime; the result is an existence claim rather than a claim about every regression problem. The examples also appear to fall outside the explanations for the peak offered by previous work.

The authors propose that the peak’s position depends on properties of both the sample covariance spectrum and its eigenvectors. This points toward the geometry and structure of the observed data as relevant alongside parameter and sample counts. The proven examples challenge an overly rigid division between under- and over-parameterized behavior, while the proposed explanation identifies a direction for understanding where the peak occurs.
neurips-2024-least-squares-regression-ca.tldr: Two proven examples show that least-squares regression can exhibit double descent even in the under-parameterized regime.

paragraphs: MathPile is a mathematics-focused corpus containing approximately 9.5 billion tokens for language-model pretraining. The project emphasizes the quality and diversity of training material, treating careful selection and processing as central parts of dataset construction. Its intended use is to strengthen mathematical reasoning in language models.

The creation pipeline includes preprocessing, preliminary filtering, language identification, cleaning, further filtering, and deduplication. The authors also check for overlap with downstream benchmark test sets and remove detected duplicates. This benchmark-contamination step addresses a concrete concern when evaluating models trained on large collections: test material may otherwise appear within the training corpus.

The authors conduct continual-pretraining experiments and report improvements on common mathematical reasoning benchmarks. Those results provide empirical support for the corpus’s usefulness in the tested training setting. They also release different corpus versions and the processing scripts, making both the training material and its preparation methods available to others. The contribution thus combines a substantial mathematical resource, a quality-focused preparation workflow, and experimental evidence of benefits.
neurips-2024-mathpile-a-billion-token-sc.tldr: MathPile offers roughly 9.5 billion carefully processed mathematics tokens and reports reasoning gains from continual pretraining.

paragraphs: This paper adapts mirror descent and preconditioned gradient descent to optimization over probability distributions in Wasserstein space. In ordinary vector optimization, these methods adjust the geometry of the update to better fit the objective. The authors investigate how to obtain analogous benefits when the objects being optimized are distributions.

Their analysis adapts relative smoothness and convexity conditions to this setting. A central difficulty is deciding along which curves through distribution space these properties should hold. With suitable choices, they prove convergence guarantees for discrete-time schemes based on Wasserstein gradients, covering new combinations of objective functionals and regularizers. The guarantees depend on the appropriate geometric conditions.

The paper illustrates why this flexibility matters through ill-conditioned optimization tasks, where adapting the geometry induced by a regularizer offers advantages. It also studies alignment of single cells in computational biology and shows improvements from choosing different discrepancies and geometries. Together, the theory and examples connect convergence analysis with practical choices about how differences between distributions should shape optimization.
neurips-2024-mirror-and-preconditioned-g.tldr: The paper extends geometry-adapted gradient methods to Wasserstein space and proves convergence under suitable relative smoothness and convexity conditions.

paragraphs: MSVMamba aims to improve the balance between computational cost and accuracy in visual state-space models. These models offer global receptive fields with complexity linear in input length, but commonly used multiple scanning directions introduce redundancy. The authors analyze why multiple scans help and identify long-range dependency learning as an important factor.

Their design scans two-dimensional feature maps at both original and reduced resolutions. This multiscale approach supports long-range relationships while reducing computation. The model also includes a convolutional feed-forward network to address insufficient mixing between feature channels. Together, these components target spatial information exchange and channel interaction while keeping the parameter budget limited.

The Tiny model reaches 83.0% top-1 accuracy on ImageNet. With Mask R-CNN and a 1x training schedule on COCO, it achieves 46.9% box mAP and 42.5% instance mAP; single-scale evaluation on ADE20K gives 47.9% mIoU. These reported results demonstrate competitive performance across classification, detection, and segmentation, supporting the proposed multiscale scanning strategy across several visual tasks.
neurips-2024-multi-scale-vmamba-hierarch.tldr: MSVMamba uses multiscale scanning and channel mixing to improve the efficiency–performance balance of visual state-space models.

paragraphs: Neural networks sometimes need to optimize objectives involving operations such as ranking or shortest paths. These objectives can be non-differentiable, so researchers replace them with continuous relaxations that supply gradients. The paper addresses a remaining difficulty: those relaxed losses can themselves be non-convex and suffer from gradients that vanish or explode.

Newton Losses use second-order information from the loss, represented through Hessian or empirical Fisher matrices, to construct a replacement training loss. The neural network still learns through gradient descent. By confining the use of curvature information to the loss construction, the method aims to improve a difficult optimization bottleneck while remaining computationally efficient.

The authors apply the approach to eight differentiable algorithms for sorting and shortest paths. They report significant gains for less-optimized algorithms and consistent improvements even for well-optimized ones. These results suggest that the behavior of the objective itself is a useful intervention point: improving how it supplies a learning signal can benefit network training without requiring second-order optimization of the entire network.
neurips-2024-newton-losses-using-curvatu.tldr: Newton Losses use loss curvature to improve difficult differentiable objectives while keeping ordinary gradient descent for network training.

paragraphs: Localized receptive fields make neurons selective for contiguous regions of their inputs. They are common in early sensory processing and can also emerge in neural networks. Existing explanations based on explicitly encouraging sparse or independent representations reproduce such fields, but do not directly explain localization when those efficiency objectives are absent.

The authors study a feed-forward network trained on a data model inspired by natural-image structure. They derive effective learning dynamics for a single nonlinear neuron to explain how localization develops during learning. Their analysis makes precise the contribution of higher-order input statistics, building on earlier work that identified non-Gaussian statistics as important.

The paper also demonstrates that predictions from the single-neuron dynamics extend to networks with many neurons. This provides an alternative account of localization based on the interaction between input structure and nonlinear learning dynamics. Its explanatory scope is the studied model and demonstrated extension, offering a possible mechanism relevant to neural circuits without requiring an explicit top-down objective for efficient coding.
neurips-2024-nonlinear-dynamics-of-local.tldr: The paper explains how higher-order input statistics and nonlinear learning dynamics can produce localized receptive fields without explicit efficiency objectives.

paragraphs: PhyRecon tackles the gap between reconstructing a scene’s appearance and recovering geometry that behaves plausibly under physics. The paper attributes shortcomings in prior implicit reconstruction methods to missing physics modeling and difficulty recovering intricate structures. Its approach trains implicit surfaces using both differentiable rendering and differentiable physical simulation.

A particle-based simulator operates with the neural representation through a proposed conversion called Surface Points Marching Cubes. This efficiently connects signed-distance-based surfaces to explicit surface points, enabling learning from both rendering and physical losses. The method also models uncertainty in rendering and physics to compensate for inaccurate or inconsistent geometric priors obtained from individual images.

Physical uncertainty additionally guides pixel sampling to improve the learning of slender structures. These components jointly connect appearance, geometry, and physical behavior during reconstruction. Experiments show improved reconstruction quality and at least a 40% improvement in physical stability across all evaluated datasets in physical simulators. The results support the value of incorporating simulation directly into the reconstruction process.
neurips-2024-phyrecon-physically-plausib.tldr: PhyRecon combines differentiable rendering and physics to reconstruct scenes with improved geometry and measured physical stability.

paragraphs: Retrieval-Retro addresses inorganic retrosynthesis: identifying precursor materials for making a target material. The paper focuses on an area where machine-learning applications have received less attention than organic retrosynthesis. Its approach uses a knowledge base to bring information from reference materials into the prediction process.

The method retrieves references using domain knowledge, including the thermodynamic relationship between the target and possible precursors. This relationship helps identify plausible precursor sets among alternatives. Attention layers then extract precursor information implicitly from the retrieved references. This learned extraction is intended to help the model construct new synthesis recipes from relevant examples instead of directly reusing their precursor information.

The authors report extensive experiments showing superior retrosynthesis-planning performance, with particular strength in discovering novel synthesis recipes. That finding matters for materials discovery because useful planning must extend beyond recipes already represented by individual references. The contribution combines domain-informed retrieval with a learned mechanism for incorporating retrieved knowledge into new predictions, linking expert chemical relationships to the model’s use of examples.
neurips-2024-retrieval-retro-retrieval-b.tldr: Retrieval-Retro combines thermodynamics-informed retrieval and attention-based knowledge extraction to improve inorganic synthesis-recipe prediction.

paragraphs: This paper investigates why detailed two-dimensional diffusion models can yield overly smooth three-dimensional shapes through Score Distillation Sampling. It connects the image guidance used in score distillation to the velocity field of a denoising generative process. This interpretation makes the choice of noise an explicit part of the explanation.

After a change of variables, SDS resembles DDIM with a higher-variance noise mechanism. SDS samples fresh independent noise at every step, whereas DDIM infers noise from previous predictions. The authors argue that the extra variance can cause unrealistic, smoothed outputs. They improve the noise approximation by inverting DDIM within each SDS update.

For two-dimensional images, this modification makes the generative process almost identical to DDIM. In three-dimensional generation, the authors report removal of over-smoothing and preservation of finer detail, bringing output quality closer to two-dimensional sampling. Experiments show quality comparable to or better than other state-of-the-art score-distillation methods, without additional neural-network training or multi-view supervision. The contribution ties a practical update rule to a clearer account of the noise dynamics.
neurips-2024-score-distillation-via-repa.tldr: Using DDIM inversion to improve SDS noise estimates reduces over-smoothing and preserves more detail in generated three-dimensional shapes.

paragraphs: This paper examines treatment-effect estimation when outcomes are recorded as high-dimensional observations in a randomized controlled trial. Randomization supplies a favorable causal setting, yet the authors theoretically show that common modeling and sampling choices can still produce biased estimates. The issue is whether the analysis accurately answers the causal question.

To investigate practical consequences, they create ISTAnt, a real-world randomized benchmark studying hygienic grooming in garden ants after microparticles are applied to colony members. They compare 6,480 models fine-tuned from modern visual backbones. The results show that sampling and modeling choices substantially affect causal-estimate accuracy, and that classification accuracy does not serve as a proxy for it.

The authors repeat the analysis on synthetic visual data with a controlled causal model, further supporting their findings. The central implication is that evaluating a representation for a scientific task requires measuring its performance on that task’s causal target. The paper consequently calls for benchmarks grounded in downstream scientific questions and offers guidelines for representation learning intended to answer causal questions.
neurips-2024-smoke-and-mirrors-in-causal.tldr: Theory and visual experiments show that common modeling choices can bias causal estimates even in randomized trials, despite strong classification performance.

paragraphs: UltraMedical addresses the shortage of specialized data for developing biomedical language models in the open-source community. The paper emphasizes that strong domain models depend on high-quality datasets, including examples suitable for preference learning. Such learning requires information about which responses are preferable in addition to ordinary training examples.

The authors assemble manually created and synthetic biomedical datasets with preference annotations involving multiple advanced language models. They use these collections to fine-tune a suite of models based on the Llama-3 family. The aim is to build specialized generalists: models with biomedical expertise while retaining a broader range of capabilities.

The paper reports strong performance across medical benchmarks and also develops reward models evaluated on biomedical and general reward benchmarks. These reward models support further online preference learning in the biomedical setting. The contribution therefore spans training data, adapted language models, and models for judging responses. Together, these resources address several parts of the development process that depend on access to specialized biomedical examples and preference information.
neurips-2024-ultramedical-building-speci.tldr: UltraMedical supplies biomedical training and preference data, fine-tuned Llama-3 models, and reward models for further preference learning.

paragraphs: This paper studies how well Transformers can approximate sequence-processing relationships that involve long, sparse, and complicated memory. The central concern is expressive power: what the architecture can represent and how that ability depends on its components. The authors approach the question through a systematic theoretical analysis of sequence modeling.

They examine dot-product self-attention, positional encoding, and feed-forward layers, considering both their individual roles and their combined effects. Explicit approximation rates give a quantitative account of how closely the model can represent the relationships under study. The analysis also identifies the roles of architectural parameters, including the number of layers and attention heads.

Experiments validate the theoretical insights, connecting the mathematical account to observed model behavior. The authors also use those insights to suggest alternative architectures. The contribution is a component-level explanation of Transformer approximation ability, supported by quantitative theory and experiments. It connects architectural choices to the demands of sequence memory, providing a basis for considering changes to how such models are constructed.
neurips-2024-understanding-the-expressiv.tldr: The paper derives approximation rates explaining how Transformer components, depth, and attention heads contribute to sequence-modeling expressiveness.
